reconcile.connective: Defenders distinguish the prohibited act (murder) from killing the commandment never covers — lawful war, self-defense, judicial execution, and the divinely decreed Amalekite war.

discrepancy.connective: Thomas Paine presses the hardest objection, arguing the divinely ordered slaughter of the Amalekites — infants and sucklings included — is murder no verbal distinction can excuse, branding such commands the work of "a book of lies, wickedness, and blasphemy."

excerpts.excerpt_text: by this law is forbidden suicide, or self-murder, parricide or murder of parents, homicide or the murder of man; yet killing of men in lawful war, or in defence of a man's self, when his own life is in danger, or the execution of malefactors by the hands or order of the civil magistrate, and killing a man at unawares, without any design, are not to be reckoned breaches of this law …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the central tension: the sixth commandment forbids murder, but explicitly does NOT cover lawful war, self-defense, or judicial execution by the civil magistrate — the very killings the Torah's legal code mandates. Truncated mid-larger-sentence (source has a semicolon, not a period) so ends with U+2026.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Nothing could justify such an exterminating decree but the absolute authority of God. This was given: all the reasons of it we do not know; but this we know well, The Judge of all the earth doth right.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Engages the genocide side of the tension: the Amalekite slaughter is reconciled with morality by appeal to God's absolute authority (divine-command harmonization), implicitly framing it as not a breach of the moral law the sixth commandment encodes. Complete source sentences ending on real periods; no ellipsis needed (lemma 'Slay both man and woman - ' trimmed as verse header).

pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this exact passage, drawing the murder-vs-lawful-killing distinction that grounds the harmonizing tradition: the sixth commandment forbids murder while expressly exempting lawful war, self-defense, and judicial execution. Used in place of Haley, whose coverage of this specific tension could not be confirmed; per spec, a harmonizing commentator surfaced on the row and keyed to the passage is preferred.
